faq.q: Why are roads built in layers?
faq.a: A tyre presses on a small patch, but soil can only take a gentle pressure. Each layer spreads the load wider, so by the time it reaches the soil the pressure is low enough not to sink the road.
Asphalt is mostly crushed stone and sand, about 95 percent, glued together with about 5 percent bitumen, a sticky black material refined from crude oil.
asks: What is the black stuff on roads?

faq.q: What do the base and sub-base do?
faq.a: These thick layers of crushed rock carry and spread the traffic load and let water drain out, so the soil underneath stays firm.
asks: What is the stone under a road for?

faq.a: The subgrade is the natural soil the road sits on, cleared, levelled and compacted. Engineers test its strength to decide how thick the layers above must be.
asks: What does a road sit on?

faq.a: Water seeps through cracks, softens the layers below and, in winter, freezes and expands. Traffic then pounds the weakened spot until pieces break away, leaving a hole.

facts: Typical asphalt is about 95 percent stone, sand and gravel bound together with about 5 percent bitumen.
Road damage rises roughly with the fourth power of axle load, a rule from the AASHO road tests of the late 1950s, so heavy lorries cause far more wear than cars.
